introduction-how-services-actually-work.core: A Service's ClusterIP isn't bound to any interface; it's a virtual IP that kube-proxy (or an eBPF replacement like Cilium) programs into every node's packet path. When a Pod connects to the ClusterIP, rules on that node DNAT the packet to one of the Service's ready endpoint Pod IPs, and conntrack keeps the connection pinned.

first_principles.problem: Engineers can't ping a ClusterIP and conclude the Service is broken.
truths: Virtual IPs exist only in rules.
Translation happens on the client's node.
derivation: Test with **curl to port**, not ping.

analogy.title: A call-forwarding number
analogy.story: The number isn't a real phone; the exchange forwards your call to an available line.
analogy.breaks: Phone exchanges are central; Service translation happens on every node independently.

example.title: Why ping fails
flow: ping 10.96.0.20 → ICMP not matched by Service rules → no reply

check.q: Why can't you usually ping a ClusterIP?
check.a: It's a virtual IP implemented only by port-specific forwarding rules, not a real interface that answers ICMP.

kube-proxy-modes-iptables-vs-ipvs.core: In iptables mode, kube-proxy writes chains of rules with random-probability matching per endpoint, which is simple but O(n) rule traversal and slow updates with thousands of Services. IPVS mode uses kernel hash tables and real load-balancing algorithms (rr, lc, sh) with O(1) lookups. nftables mode is the modern successor, and eBPF replacements (Cilium) bypass kube-proxy entirely.

first_principles.problem: A cluster with 10,000 Services takes minutes to apply rule changes and adds latency.
truths: eBPF can implement load balancing in-kernel efficiently.
derivation: **eBPF kube-proxy replacement** for performance and visibility.

analogy.title: Searching a paper list versus an index
analogy.story: Reading names one by one gets slow; an index finds them instantly.
analogy.breaks: Lists don't change often; Service endpoints change constantly, so update speed matters too.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: See how each mode implements Services.

code.text:
iptables-save -t nat | grep KUBE-SVC | head
ipvsadm -Ln | head -20
conntrack -L | wc -l

check.q: Why does IPVS scale better than iptables for many Services?
check.a: It uses hash tables for O(1) lookup instead of traversing long rule chains.

the-packet-flow-a-service-requests-journ.core: A Pod calls api.shop: DNS resolves via CoreDNS to the ClusterIP; the packet leaves the Pod's veth into the node; kube-proxy/eBPF DNATs it to a backend Pod IP; the CNI routes it (same node via bridge, other node via overlay or native routing); the backend replies and conntrack reverses the translation. Each hop is a debugging checkpoint.

first_principles.problem: A request times out and nobody knows which hop failed.
truths: Each layer has its own tools.

analogy.title: Tracing a parcel through depots
analogy.story: Was the address right, did it reach the sorting hub, the van, the door?
analogy.breaks: Parcels have tracking numbers; packets need tcpdump and logs at each hop.

code.text:
kubectl exec -it client -- nslookup api.shop
kubectl get endpointslices -n shop -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
kubectl exec -it client -- curl -m2 10.244.3.7:8080/health   # direct Pod IP
kubectl get networkpolicy -n shop

check.q: If DNS resolves but the Service has no endpoints, what's the likely cause?
check.a: No Pods match the selector or none are ready (e.g. failing readiness probes).

cni-the-plugin-that-wires-pods-together.core: When a Pod sandbox starts, the runtime calls the CNI plugin with the network namespace path: it creates a veth pair (one end in the Pod as eth0, one on the host), assigns an IP via IPAM, sets routes and installs datapath rules (bridge, overlay, eBPF). On deletion it releases the IP. Config lives in /etc/cni/net.d and binaries in /opt/cni/bin.

first_principles.problem: New Pods stay in ContainerCreating with 'failed to setup network' errors.
truths: Each Pod needs plumbing at creation.
Config and binaries must be on every node.
derivation: Inspect **veth and routes** on the node.

analogy.title: An electrician wiring each new office
analogy.story: Running cable from the wall socket into the office and labelling it with an extension number.
analogy.breaks: Electricians work for hours; CNI plumbs Pods in milliseconds.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Verify Pod plumbing on the host.

code.text:
ls /etc/cni/net.d /opt/cni/bin
ip -br link | grep -E 'veth|lxc|cali'
ip route | grep 10.244

check.q: What does a CNI plugin create to connect a Pod to the host network?
check.a: A veth pair, with one end in the Pod's network namespace and one on the host.

debugging-cni-failures.core: CNI failures show up as Pods stuck in ContainerCreating, Pods with no IP, cross-node traffic failing or intermittent drops. Debug in order: events (FailedCreatePodSandBox), CNI agent Pods and logs, IPAM availability, node routes and MTU, encapsulation ports blocked by firewalls (VXLAN UDP 8472/4789, BGP 179), and kernel modules or eBPF requirements.

first_principles.problem: Pods on the same node can talk, but cross-node Pod traffic silently fails after a firewall change.
truths: MTU issues break large packets only.

analogy.title: Diagnosing a phone network fault
analogy.story: Calls work within one building but fail between buildings, so check the trunk line.
analogy.breaks: Phone faults are usually total; MTU issues let small packets through and drop large ones.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Lower Pod MTU to underlay MTU minus encapsulation overhead.

code.text:
kubectl exec -it a -- ping -c3 -M do -s 1400 10.244.5.9   # fails?
kubectl exec -it a -- ping -c3 -M do -s 1200 10.244.5.9   # works → MTU too high

check.q: What symptom suggests an MTU mismatch?
check.a: Small packets (pings, handshakes) succeed but large transfers hang or fail.
